claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Phase evolution during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure is governed by thermally activated atomic ordering.
Redistribution and sublattice ordering of Al within the BCC matrix triggers nucleation of ordered intermediate phases.
The ordered intermediate phases may have B2-type ordering.
Ordered intermediate phases subsequently evolve into more complex low-temperature phases.
Rapidly quenched samples and identical slow-cooled or intermediate-temperature-held samples provide the controlled comparison.
Slow cooling or isothermal holding near 600–700°C provides sufficient atomic mobility for ordering.
Rapid quenching suppresses the ordering kinetics and bypasses the ordering stage.
Short- to medium-range B2-like or related ordered regions within the BCC matrix are the structural mediator.
During slow cooling or intermediate-temperature exposure, Al and possibly other species redistribute into ordered clusters or sublattices.
Local ordering lowers the free energy and thereby promotes nucleation of intermediate ordered phases.
Rapid quenching leads to retention of metastable, largely disordered BCC material.
Relative to quenched samples, slow-cooled or isothermally held samples should show diffraction and microstructural signatures of ordered intermediate phases such as B2.
Ordering may produce mechanical-property changes relative to the rapidly quenched baseline.
The extent of phase transformation should correlate systematically with the measured degree of ordering.
The proposed mechanism may not govern phase behavior when quenching suppresses diffusion or when strain or deformation dominates.
Failure of slow cooling or 600–700°C holding to produce superlattice reflections, thermal events, or microstructural differences relative to quenched samples would falsify the ordering hypothesis.
